full_judgment: 7. In this context the Learned Attorney- General Mr Hasan Ariff has submitted that there was reasonable basis for the issuance of the impugned notice in Annexure-'1' under section 150 of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act'). The Learned Attorney-General has submitted that the validity of the impugned notice could, however, indeed be challenged by the petitioner under the relevant provisions on revision of section 149 of the Act, but this the petitioners opted not to do. Failing that, it is evident to this Court that this application has been filed primarily out of an apprehension or fear of a future contingency of a possible demolition of the construction on the said plot. In that context, it is not clear to this Court the extent to which the issuance of the impugned notice in Annexure-'1' constitutes a violation of the petitioners' fundamental rights that can be challenged in Writ Jurisdiction. This Court, in agreement with the submission of the Learned Attorney-General to that effect, notes that the petitioners appear to be saying that they have a legal right not to be saddled with the impugned notice and that the respondent No.3 is under a corresponding legal duty not to issue the said notice or is not competent to issue the same. This Court is inclined to hold that in the facts and circumstances of this case there is nothing to substantiate that position adopted by the petitioners. This Court, therefore, finds that the impugned notice in Annexure-'1' is valid as having been made with lawful authority. Accordingly, this Court is of the view that it would be best for the petitioners to pursue the matter as raised in the impugned notice through the process and the proper forum reflected in the said impugned notice.
